doc.title: Henry Johnson interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 30, 1995

title: Jazz versus rock guitar: tone and dynamics
summary: Johnson contrasts jazz's pure tone and dynamics, controlled with the picking hand, against rock's distortion and constant volume.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: I want to ask you, can you delineate for us if I’m having some students that are going to be watching this video. Tell us some differences between, like in terms of your tone quality and of the volume, and maybe even what you do in the left hand, between jazz guitar playing and rock guitar playing. Now I will tell you this. I met a rock guitar player. I was in a music store trying out an instrument and he was in there kind of banging away with big bar chords and stuff. And I told him, you know, you need to listen to some jazz guitar players. I saw the guy again a little later, and he says, “Man I’m really beginning to like jazz now.” He says, “Now I know all the notes that were missing.” But give us some examples of differences between jazz and rock.

Well, jazz is like to me it’s probably the ultimate music to play because it’s the type of music that you can find your own identity in. Rock & roll, they use a lot of the loud guitars, and a lot of distortion. And the distortion is exactly what it says, it distorts the tone. So with jazz I’m looking for the purest tone I can get. Because that’s going to allow my own identity to come out in that in the dynamics. When I work with Joe, and playing jazz on my own, the music to me has to have peaks and valleys. Because you don’t breathe the same way all of the time. You don’t feel the same way all of the time. So music to me should not start here, continue here and end here. Then it’s just very flat. But you know if it starts here and it goes here and it goes down here and goes here and goes there, that’s the dynamics in the music. That’s what made Ahmad Jamal so great and Oscar Peterson, you know? All of those kind of groups. They all had dynamics. Even classical music has dynamics written in it. You know because the dynamics is part of your flowing emotions. And as far as playing the guitar, the dynamics, I find, for myself, is in my picking hand. I can pick soft, I can pick loud. But if my guitar is this loud, so it allows me to play harder, to play softer, to play middle, to play down the middle of the

beat. I can do all of those things just by doing this with my hand and my arm. But the rock players, they just crank it up and that’s where it is. And it stays that way the whole night. Pounding, pounding, pounding your ear. And to me, music should caress you and move you in different parts and make you go on different adventures, and you can’t do that without dynamics.
